stories.headline: Nepal flood: For centuries, flood-hit corridor was key route of Himalayan trade
stories.title: Nepal flood: For centuries, flood-hit corridor was key route of Himalayan trade
stories.summary: Long before trucks climbed Bhote Koshi valley, mule caravans carried rice and other grain from Nepal north to Gyirong, where traders exchanged them for Tibetan salt and wool. Salt, highly valued in Nepal’s middle hills, travelled farther south towards India. Newar merchant communities also settled in Tibetan trading towns. Nepalese troops later used the route during invasions of Tibet in 1788 and 1791 before Chinese and Tibetan forces counter-attacked in 1792.

opening: Iran won't allow military vessels to transit through the Strait of Hormuz under an agreement that the Islamic Republic is negotiating with Oman, Iran's deputy foreign minister said.
The top diplomats of the two countries met to discuss managing commercial shipping traffic in the vital waterway, which remains largely shut down nearly six months after the Iran war began.
body: Also read: Iran, Oman reach deal on Strait of Hormuz, but reopening hinges on US conditions.
Meanwhile, Israeli strikes in Gaza continued, testing the already fragile ceasefire with Hamas.
Here's a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East.
Full coverage can be found here.

No military vessels in the strait, Iran saysIran and Oman have reached a potential agreement for managing ship traffic in the Strait of Hormuz that would exclude military vessels from traversing the vital waterway.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told state television late Tuesday that commercial shipping traffic into the Persian Gulf would pass through Iranian waters, while the outbound route would pass partly through Iranian waters and partly through Oman's waters.
He said the routes would be temporary, and that Iran and Oman must discuss a permanent maritime traffic plan within 30 to 60 days.
U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way," as his administration opposes parts of the evolving deal.
Trump isn't in a hurry to resume talks with Iran.

The U.S. president told Al Jazeera over the phone on Wednesday that he believes the United States is "winning very big" as the conflict with Iran nears the six-month mark." I have no time schedule; whatever it takes," he told the Qatar-based broadcaster.
In another interview Wednesday, Trump said he thinks Iran's supreme leader, Ayatollah Motjaba Khamenei, is "very seriously wounded," but not dead.
Motjaba Khamenei became supreme leader after his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed at the start of the war.
The younger Khamenei was badly wounded in the attacks and has remained out of public view.
Israel launches a deadly strike in Gaza, health officials say.
An Israeli strike on a tent for displaced people on Wednesday in southern Gaza killed one person and wounded at least four, the territory's Health Ministry officials said.
The Israeli military said that it struck a "military operative," without elaborating.
Palestinians in the Gaza Strip have reported a surge in deadly Israeli strikes, despite a fragile ceasefire in the nearly three-year Israel-Hamas war.
Israel has said that it targets Hamas and other militants.

Gaza peace board chief criticizes Israeli strikesNickolay Mladenov, head of Trump's Board of Peace, told the U.N. Security Council on Wednesday that the gbetween what has been agreed by both sides and what is happening on the ground is the biggest risk to the peace process in Gaza." Israeli strikes have continued since the roadmap was accepted, and Palestinian civilians are still being killed," Mladenov said.

While the ceasefire is holding and casualties have fallen sharply, he added, a ceasefire where "civilians are still buried is not yet one that the people of Gaza can really feel." Also read: Iran and Oman discuss temporary Hormuz corridor as impasse with US drags onIsrael insists Hamas must disarm first.

Israel's deputy U.N. ambassador Noa Furman told the Security Council on Wednesday that Israel is committed to Trump's 20-point peace plan but that Hamas' "disarmament must come first" before Gaza's reconstruction can begin.
She added that Israel was working closely with the U.S. and the Board of Peace to achieve this.
Children's kites in Gaza dismantled over Israeli threats.
Some parents said children in Gaza are dismantling their kites after Israel threatened to ramp up strikes as the toys keep flying into southern Israel.
In the past, kites and balloons have been set aflame and launched across the Gaza border, igniting fields and property in Israeli communities.
The Palestinian militant group Hamas has downplayed the danger the kites pose.

In tents near the Mediterranean Sea in southern Gaza, kids dismantled the plastic, cloth and wood contraptions as adults looked on." They've lost their simple dreams, their education, their childhood, the simple things they used to enjoy," lamented resident Atiya Abu Samhan.

Israel has legalized more than 100 settlements since 2022Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Tuesday that his government, in an effort to ensure Israel's existence, has legalized more than 104 settlements and established 160 farming outposts in the West Bank since he took office again in 2022.
Israeli settlements in the West Bank are largely considered illegal, but Netanyahu has made their expansion a priority in the lead-up to Israel's upcoming election.
About 3 million Palestinians live alongside more than 500,000 Israeli settlers in the occupied territory, which has seen a recent spike in violence as the Israeli presence expands.

Dubai airport traffic dropped sharply during Iran warDubai International Airport, one of the world's busiest travel hubs, said Wednesday that it saw a sharp drop in passengers as the Iran war disrupted air travel across the Middle East.
The airport recorded 13 million passengers in the second quarter of 2026, bringing the total to about 31.5 million passengers for the first half of the year.
That's down 31.3% compared to last year at the halfway mark.

Iran's top diplomat slams new US sanctions threatForeign Minister Abbas Araghchi in a letter to the United Nations on Tuesday urged the world body to condemn the latest U.S. move to cut off Tehran from the rest of the global economy.

The " economic onslaught " that U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent declared this week amounts to the deliberate targeting of Iranian civilians with the "intentional deprivation of access to food, medicines, medical equipment, energy and other necessities," according to Araghchi." Silence in the face of such systematic coercion risks further normalizing violations of the U.N. Charter and principles of international law," Araghchi wrote in the letter, obtained by The Associated Press.
USS Lincoln stopping in Thailand after long deployment.

The U.S. aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln will make a stop in Thailand after its grueling deployment in the Middle East, Thai officials said Tuesday, without specifying a date or port for security reasons.
The Lincoln's lengthy record-setting deployment during the Iran war has raised concerns about deteriorating mental health among the crew.

stories.headline: The story behind the English translation of Gulabnama
stories.title: The story behind the English translation of Gulabnama
stories.summary: Gulabnama is the biography of Maharaja Gulab Singh, the founder of the Dogra dynasty of Jammu and Kashmir. Originally written in Persian by Diwan Kirpa Ram, the work chronicles the establishment of the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir in 1846 and traces the life and political career of Maharaja Gulab Singh. It offers valuable insights into his statecraft, administrative policies, and the strategies he employed to consolidate and safeguard the frontiers of his kingdom during a turbulent period. Initially, Maharaja Gulab Singh was reluctant to have his life documented, fearing that sensitive family matters and personal details might be made public. For this reason, he was unwilling to entrust the task to the court historian, Ganesh Das Badhera. Instead, the responsibility was later assigned to Diwan Kirpa Ram, the son of Dewan Jawala Sahai, who served as Gulab Singh’s Prime Minister. The book faced significant hurdles in reaching the public. It took over a century for it to be accessible to common readers. Diwan Kirpa Ram completed the draft by roughly 1865-1866, but it was not printed until 1875 in Srinagar. It was finally published in 1875 at the Tofa Printing Press in Srinagar, Kashmir. However, it became rare quickly, and various attempts to translate it into English over next century were unsuccessful due to fundings, translation quality and institutional hurdles. Recognizing its historical importance, Raja Amar Singh, the father of Maharaja Hari Singh, wrote to Maharaja Pratap Singh in 1901, recommending that an annual budget of Rs. 500–1,000 be set aside for translating and publishing Gulabnama. Unfortunately, the proposal could not be implemented because no suitable translator could be found. A similar effort had earlier been undertaken for Kalhana’s Rajatarangini, which had been translated into English by M. A. Stein. The government sanctioned about Rs. 3,000 for that project, with nearly Rs. 1,500 spent on paper, printing, and distribution. This demonstrates the state’s willingness to invest in publishing important historical works. Professor Arnold of the University of Lahore was the first scholar approached to translate Gulabnama into English. However, after translating only the first sixty pages, he abandoned the project for personal reasons. The search for a competent translator continued. In 1902, Raja Amar Singh again approached Maharaja Pratap Singh, who constituted a committee to supervise the translation. Raja Amar Singh served as its President, while Diwan Diya Krishna, Bhagwan Narayan Das, and Dr. Suraj Bal were appointed as members. The committee engaged Babu Jagadish Chandra Banerjee to prepare an English translation for publication in Calcutta and paid an advance of Rs. 500. However, his translation was later rejected because it did not accurately reflect the original Persian text of Diwan Kirpa Ram. Another attempt was made during 1915–16 under Maharaja Pratap Singh, but it also remained unsuccessful. Later, efforts were made to translate the work into Urdu and Sanskrit, but these projects likewise remained incomplete. A major breakthrough came when Professor Sukhdev Singh Charak, Principal of Himachal Pradesh University, voluntarily undertook the English translation. He began the work in 1965 and completed it in 1976, devoting eleven years to the task. A benevolent man who appreciated the importance of the work offered Professor Charak a grant of Rs. 5,000. However, the total cost of publication was estimated at around Rs. 12,000. He was advised to seek financial assistance from the Jammu and Kashmir Academy of Art, Culture and Languages, but the Academy declined to provide funding. In 1975, Professor Charak was involved in a severe accident that left him critically injured. At the time, he felt that his survival was uncertain and that he might only have a few hours left to live. Facing what he believed to be the end of his life, he reached out to ensure that his life’s mission the translation of this book would be fulfilled. He even wrote a letter to a contact expressing that it was his final wish to have the book published. Fortunately, Professor Charak survived his injuries. Following his recovery, he returned to Jammu in 1976 to finalize the manuscript. The book was subsequently sent to the printing press later that year, finally appearing in 1977. The English translation of Gulabnama was formally released by Dr. Karan Singh, bringing to fruition a project that had witnessed more than seven decades of unsuccessful attempts. Author’s Note: This article was inspired by a YouTube video on The Dispatch by Zafar Choudhary. Hilal Ahmad Tantray, Research Scholar, Department of History and Culture, Jamia Millia Islamia, New Delhi.

stories.headline: 5% GST pushing Kashmir’s walnut industry to brink: Growers
stories.title: 5% GST pushing Kashmir’s walnut industry to brink: Growers
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 26: The walnut industry in Kashmir, which provides livelihood to thousands of farming families, is facing a serious crisis due to increasing competition from imported walnuts, taxation, inadequate research support and poor market infrastructure, the Fruit Association has said in a representation to Chief Minister Omar Abdullah. Haji Bhadur Khan, President of the Fruit Association, has sought immediate government intervention to safeguard Kashmir's traditional walnut industry, saying the sector was being pushed towards the brink of collapse by a combination of policy shortcomings, foreign competition and inadequate institutional support. Khan said walnut growers in Kashmir are predominantly small and economically vulnerable farmers, many of whom live in far-flung areas and depend heavily on the seasonal crop for their livelihood. "The 5 per cent GST imposed on walnuts has added to the financial burden on growers and made locally produced walnuts less competitive in the market," he said. Khan urged the government to reduce GST on walnuts to zero per cent, arguing that the move would provide relief to growers and help revive the sector. The Fruit Association president also raised concern over the growing influx of walnuts from China, Chile and California, saying cheaper imported produce was adversely affecting the market for Kashmiri walnuts. Referring particularly to China's "185" walnut variety, Khan said China had witnessed a significant increase in production and exports over the past decade. He said Chinese walnuts, known for their large kernel size, high yield and competitive prices, had gained presence in the Indian market, making it increasingly difficult for local growers to compete. "Chile had also emerged as a major player in the global walnut market, supplying high-quality walnuts at comparatively lower prices, while California had strengthened its position through advanced farming techniques, sophisticated processing facilities and aggressive marketing," he said. Khan called for appropriate protective measures, including restrictions or tariffs on imported walnuts, to protect domestic growers and encourage the consumption of locally produced walnuts. He also flagged concerns over the alleged under-valuation of imported walnuts for tariff purposes, saying such practices further put local producers at a disadvantage. Another major concern raised by Khan was the alleged lack of research and development support for Kashmir's walnut sector. He said there was an urgent need to develop improved walnut varieties and enhance kernel quality and productivity. "The Department of Horticulture has played no role in developing new walnut varieties or improving kernel quality," Khan alleged in the representation, calling for dedicated research centres focused on walnut cultivation. He also sought technical guidance and training for farmers on modern cultivation practices, including the development of high-yielding and disease-resistant varieties. Poor market infrastructure is another issue faced by farmers. Khan said walnut markets in Kashmir, including the major market at Kupwara, lacked adequate basic facilities such as clean and hygienic storage spaces, reliable electricity and water supply. He urged the government to upgrade walnut market infrastructure, improve hygiene and storage facilities and ensure uninterrupted power and water supply to walnut processing units. Khan further alleged that officials had shown little interest in addressing these issues and called for accountability for what he described as mismanagement and negligence.The Association president sought permission for construction of a second storey on allotted shops at Kupwara Mandi, saying the additional space was required for the purchase and repacking of walnut kernels, expansion of business operations and accommodation of growing customer demand. Khan urged the authorities to examine the alleged import of walnuts and walnut products through Nepal to avoid taxes, claiming that products originating from China and other countries were entering the market through such routes and causing losses to Kashmiri producers. He sought reduction of GST, protective measures against unfair foreign competition, establishment of walnut-focused research centres, farmer training, development of improved varieties and modernisation of market infrastructure. Khan said the walnut industry was not merely an economic activity but "a way of life for thousands of families" across Kashmir. "The combined impact of high GST, foreign competition, official apathy and poor infrastructure has pushed this industry to the brink of collapse," Khan said, urging the government to take immediate and concrete measures to protect Kashmir's walnut growers and revive the industry. He sought government response to the challenges confronting the walnut sector, with particular emphasis on making Kashmiri walnuts more competitive, strengthening domestic production and protecting the livelihoods of growers dependent on the crop.

Srinagar, Aug 26: The walnut industry in Kashmir, which provides livelihood to thousands of farming families, is facing a serious crisis due to increasing competition from imported walnuts, taxation, inadequate research support and poor market infrastructure, the Fruit Association has said in a representation to Chief Minister Omar Abdullah.

The Fruit Association president also raised concern over the growing influx of walnuts from China, Chile and California, saying cheaper imported produce was adversely affecting the market for Kashmiri walnuts.

The Association president sought permission for construction of a second storey on allotted shops at Kupwara Mandi, saying the additional space was required for the purchase and repacking of walnut kernels, expansion of business operations and accommodation of growing customer demand.

stories.headline: Supreme Court judge seeks transfer of Rajasthan High Court acting Chief Justice, CJI says allegations can’t be treated as a finding
stories.title: Supreme Court judge seeks transfer of Rajasthan High Court acting Chief Justice, CJI says allegations can’t be treated as a finding
stories.summary: CJI Surya Kant says that the matter is being examined at the appropriate level and that the process will take into account the material placed by Justice Mehta as well as the response of Justice Sharma
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence

article_sentences: In three letters to Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, Supreme Court judge Justice Sandeep Mehta this month asked why his “fervent appeals” for the transfer of Rajasthan High Court Acting Chief Justice (ACJ) Sanjeev Prakash Sharma have been “ignored” despite there being “clear evidence” of “favouritism”.

In a press statement released by the Supreme Court following media reports on August 26 about Justice Mehta's letters, Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, who is currently abroad on an official tour, emphasised that he has already taken note of the concerns raised by Justice Mehta in his letters, and stressed that "allegations against a sitting judge must be dealt with strictly through the established institutional mechanism".

The CJI maintained that the contents of the letters cannot be adjudicated in the public domain and that the judge concerned must be given a fair opportunity to place his response before any conclusion was reached.

“Any decision regarding the continuation, transfer or other administrative action concerning the acting Chief Justice would be taken by the competent institutional authority after due consideration of the material… The Supreme Court cannot allow individual complaints concerning judges to be determined through competing claims in the media,” the statement read.
In his first letter on August 2, 2026, Justice Mehta had written to the CJI about the “grim and disturbing scenario” in his parent High Court in Rajasthan.

In the letter, he said the ACJ of the High Court, who is due to retire on September 26, displayed a total lack of leadership qualities and exhibited conduct unbecoming of a leader of the institution on more than one occasion.
The Supreme Court judge reminded the CJI that he had been making repeated requests for the appointment of a regular Chief Justice to the High Court since the beginning of 2026.
“However, till date, the request to have a Chief Justice from another State in my parent High Court has met with no positive response,” Justice Mehta wrote.
He said there was maladministration and malpractices on both the judicial and administrative side of the High Court.

The next letter, on August 10, noted that the CJI had asked Justice Sharma to respond to the shifting of cases, but said that no specific information was further available on the reply or facts of these cases.
Justice Mehta wrote that he had "positive information"that Justice Sharma called and humiliated judicial officers in Rajasthan to satisfy a “personal vendetta”.
A full court meeting was organised to designate a “large number of favoured advocates as seniors”, that too, on a working day, he accused.

stories.headline: Repeated closures undermine Mughal Road’s promise as Kashmir’s alternate highway
stories.title: Repeated closures undermine Mughal Road’s promise as Kashmir’s alternate highway
stories.summary: Shopian, Aug 26: The Mughal Road, touted as an alternative link between Kashmir and the Jammu region, has faced repeated disruptions this summer due to cloudbursts and landslides, raising questions over its reliability as an all-weather route. On August 5, Chief Minister Omar Abdullah travelled to Rajouri and Poonch through the historic road and later described its condition as worse than the Jammu-Srinagar National Highway, which had itself been battered by torrential rain and landslides. The Mughal Road connects south Kashmir’s Shopian district with Poonch in the Jammu region, cutting across the Pir Panjal range. The road was thrown open to vehicular traffic in 2009 and was projected as an alternative link to the Jammu-Srinagar National Highway. However, repeated weather-related disruptions have limited its potential as a dependable alternative route. Since June, the road has witnessed several cloudbursts and landslides. Official records show that a cloudburst occurred at Zaznar Point on June 29, while another hit the Sukh Sarai area on June 14. A landslide was subsequently reported in the Lal Ghulam area on July 14, followed by another in the Sukh Sarai area on August 3, disrupting traffic along the route. Despite the repeated incidents, authorities have been working to restore connectivity at the earliest. An official from the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) said the 52 RCC under Project Beacon has been clearing the road immediately after blockages. “Our teams respond immediately whenever the road is blocked. The priority is to clear debris and restore traffic at the earliest,” the official said. The road’s vulnerability, however, is not limited to the summer months. Mughal Road remains closed for more than four months during winter because of heavy snowfall around Peer Ki Gali, located at an elevation of around 11,500 feet. The seasonal closure limits its usefulness as a reliable alternative to the national highway, particularly during periods when the main Jammu-Srinagar route is disrupted. For residents and traders in Shopian, Rajouri and Poonch, the road is an important connectivity link, providing a shorter route between the two regions. “The road is important for people on both sides of the Pir Panjal, but frequent closures make it difficult to depend on it for regular travel and transportation,” said Mohammad Ashraf, a local resident. The route also has economic significance for south Kashmir’s horticulture sector, as it provides access to markets in the Jammu region. The repeated disruptions have assumed greater significance as the Jammu-Srinagar National Highway itself remains vulnerable to landslides, shooting stones and extreme weather. Mughal Road could provide an important alternative during such disruptions, particularly for traffic between south Kashmir and the Pir Panjal districts. But its own exposure to cloudbursts, landslides and heavy snowfall limits the extent to which it can perform that role. However, officials said that a proposed 9-km tunnel between Chatta Pani in Poonch and Zaznar in Shopian could eventually address the Mughal Road’s biggest weakness of its prolonged winter closures and vulnerability to extreme weather. The Centre approved the Pir Ki Gali tunnel project in June 2025 at an estimated cost of around Rs 3830 crore, with the tunnel envisaged as an all-weather link between the Kashmir Valley and the Pir Panjal region. “Once completed, it would bypass the high-altitude Pir Ki Gali stretch, where heavy snowfall regularly disrupts traffic for several months,” said the officials.
